questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity to look up a key in a Swift Dictionary?

options.text: O(1) constant time because the hash leads directly to the bucket.
options.explanation: Right. Hash functions map keys to buckets for instant O(1) average lookup.

options.text: O(n) linear time because Swift scans every bucket from start to end.
options.explanation: Swift does not scan every element. It jumps directly to the hashed bucket.

options.text: O(log n) logarithmic time because the keys are kept in a binary tree.
options.explanation: Swift Dictionary uses a hash table rather than a binary search tree.

options.text: O(n log n) time because the collection sorts itself on every query.
options.explanation: Dictionaries are unordered and do not sort keys during lookups.

questions.prompt: Which protocol must a type conform to before it can serve as a Dictionary key?

options.text: Comparable, so Swift can arrange keys in ascending order.
options.explanation: Dictionary keys are unordered and do not require Comparable conformance.

options.text: Hashable, which provides an integer hash value and Equatable checks.
options.explanation: Right. Hashable provides the hash integer to place keys into buckets.

options.text: Codable, so Swift can convert the keys to JSON strings automatically.
options.explanation: Codable handles serialization, not internal hash table bucket indexing.

options.text: Identifiable, so SwiftUI views can loop over the keys without indices.
options.explanation: Identifiable is for view identification, not dictionary key hashing.

questions.prompt: What happens when two different keys produce the exact same bucket index?

options.text: The program crashes immediately with a fatal hash collision error.
options.explanation: Collisions are normal in hash tables and do not cause crashes.

options.text: Swift automatically overwrites the earlier value with the new value.
options.explanation: Different keys do not overwrite each other when their hashes collide.

options.text: A collision occurs, and Swift resolves it using probing techniques.
options.explanation: Right. Swift detects the occupied bucket and finds another open slot.

options.text: Swift converts the whole dictionary into a linked list permanently.
options.explanation: Swift uses open addressing within the table rather than converting types.

questions.prompt: Why is storing hashValue to disk or a network database dangerous in Swift?

options.text: Because hash values in Swift are always negative numbers on 64-bit devices.
options.explanation: Hash values can be positive or negative integers.

options.text: Because Swift encrypts hash values using private keys that expire daily.
options.explanation: Swift does not use private cryptographic keys for hash values.

options.text: Because hash values exceed the maximum integer size supported by JSON.
options.explanation: Hash values are standard Int integers that fit in 64-bit numbers.

options.text: Because Swift randomizes hash seeds per run, changing values on launch.
options.explanation: Right. SipHash seeds are random per process, so values change on restart.

questions.prompt: What is the core rule connecting Equatable and Hashable in Swift?

options.text: If two instances are equal with ==, they must produce equal hash values.
options.explanation: Right. Equal instances must feed the exact same data into the hasher.

options.text: If two instances have equal hash values, they must be equal with ==.
options.explanation: Different objects can have the same hash value due to collisions.

options.text: Any type that implements Equatable automatically gets Hashable synthesized.
options.explanation: Equatable alone does not synthesize Hashable; stored properties must conform.

options.text: Types must hash every property, even properties excluded from == checks.
options.explanation: Hashing properties ignored by == violates the Hashable contract.

questions.prompt: How does using a hash table optimize the classic Two Sum interview problem?

options.text: It eliminates the need for any additional memory storage entirely.
options.explanation: A hash table uses O(n) auxiliary space to store visited values.

options.text: It checks for the complement in O(1) time, reducing total time to O(n).
options.explanation: Right. Checking complement existence in O(1) replaces nested loops.

options.text: It sorts the incoming numbers in O(1) time before starting the search.
options.explanation: Comparison sorting requires at least O(n log n) time.

options.text: It splits the array into two halves and runs binary search across both.
options.explanation: Two Sum with a hash table scans once without binary searching.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of looking up a value in a hash table?

options.text: O(1) constant time, because hash tables never slow down under load.
options.explanation: Worst-case time is not constant when collisions pile up in buckets.

options.text: O(log n) time, because collisions form a balanced search tree inside.
options.explanation: Standard open-addressing hash tables do not balance into trees.

options.text: O(n) linear time, if all inserted keys collide into the same bucket.
options.explanation: Right. Severe collisions force the table to inspect every stored entry.

options.text: O(n^2) quadratic time, because comparing keys requires nested loops.
options.explanation: Inspecting n items in a bucket takes linear O(n) time, not quadratic.

questions.prompt: What happens if you mutate an object while it is used as a key in a Set?

options.text: Swift automatically recalculates the hash and moves it to a new bucket.
options.explanation: Swift does not observe mutations or relocate keys automatically.

options.text: The set throws a compiler warning and freezes the mutated property.
options.explanation: The compiler cannot detect runtime mutations of reference objects.

options.text: The object is instantly deleted from the set to avoid memory corruption.
options.explanation: Sets do not delete elements when their properties change.

options.text: The object sits in the wrong bucket, causing future lookups to fail.
options.explanation: Right. The set searches the new hash bucket, missing the stored item.

questions.prompt: Which syntax safely updates a character counter in a Swift dictionary?

options.text: counts[char, default: 0] += 1 to provide a fallback value for missing keys.
options.explanation: Right. The default parameter provides 0 if the key is not yet present.

options.text: counts[char]++ without unwrapping the optional integer value first.
options.explanation: Subscript access returns an optional, so ++ will not compile directly.

options.text: counts.append(char) to add the character count to the end of the table.
options.explanation: Dictionaries do not have an append method because they are unordered.

options.text: counts.increment(key: char) to trigger automatic atomic counter updates.
options.explanation: Dictionary has no increment method in the Swift standard library.

questions.prompt: When does the Swift compiler automatically synthesize Hashable conformance?

options.text: For all classes that inherit from NSObject in an iOS application.
options.explanation: NSObject uses pointer hashing, not synthesized Swift Hashable.

options.text: For structs and enums whose stored properties all conform to Hashable.
options.explanation: Right. Structs and enums get automatic synthesis if members conform.

options.text: For any custom type that declares at least one integer identifier.
options.explanation: Automatic synthesis requires all stored properties to conform.

options.text: Only when the developer manually defines the hash(into:) method.
options.explanation: Manual implementation is optional if all properties already conform.

questions.prompt: How does a Set differ from an Array in Swift when checking membership?

options.text: Set takes O(n) linear time, while Array takes O(1) constant time.
options.explanation: Array contains takes O(n), while Set contains takes O(1) average time.

options.text: Set requires sorting items first, while Array searches without sorting.
options.explanation: Set does not require sorting; it uses hash buckets for fast lookups.

options.text: Set checks membership in O(1) average time, while Array takes O(n).
options.explanation: Right. Set uses a hash table to jump directly to the item bucket.

options.text: Set and Array both take O(log n) time to check element existence.
options.explanation: Neither collection uses binary search by default for contains calls.

questions.prompt: Why can you not rely on the iteration order of a Swift Dictionary?

options.text: Because Swift reverses dictionary ordering on every second iteration.
options.explanation: Swift does not alternate iteration direction between loop calls.

options.text: Because dictionary order is decided by the alphabetical order of values.
options.explanation: Dictionary iteration does not sort by values or keys.

options.text: Because ARC deallocates empty buckets while loops are still running.
options.explanation: ARC manages memory lifetimes, not collection iteration traversal.

options.text: Because hash table bucket layout and randomized seeds determine order.
options.explanation: Right. Dictionaries are unordered; items depend on bucket placement.

questions.prompt: What optimization avoids frequent rehashing when creating large dictionaries?

options.text: Calling reserveCapacity to preallocate enough buckets in advance.
options.explanation: Right. Preallocating bucket storage prevents expensive resize passes.

options.text: Turning off Hashable synthesis by providing custom static hash integers.
options.explanation: Static hash values cause severe collisions and degrade performance.

options.text: Wrapping dictionary keys in autorelease pools before inserting them.
options.explanation: Autorelease pools manage Objective-C objects, not hash table sizes.

options.text: Sorting all incoming keys before adding them to the dictionary.
options.explanation: Sorting does not prevent rehashing and adds unnecessary O(n log n) work.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift randomize hash seeds with SipHash on every app execution?

options.text: To compress dictionary memory footprints by fifty percent on iOS.
options.explanation: Randomizing seeds does not compress the memory storage footprint.

options.text: To prevent collision denial-of-service attacks from malicious inputs.
options.explanation: Right. Attackers cannot craft keys that force worst-case O(n) bucket collisions.

options.text: To make sure that dictionaries always sort keys in order.
options.explanation: Random seeds make iteration order non-deterministic rather than sorted.

options.text: To allow multiple threads to mutate the same dictionary simultaneously.
options.explanation: Dictionary is not thread-safe; mutating across threads causes data races.

questions.prompt: What happens if a custom Hashable type hashes a property that is ignored by ==?

options.text: The Swift compiler rejects the struct with a fatal syntax check error.
options.explanation: The compiler cannot verify that hash(into:) matches == logic.

options.text: The type automatically defaults to memory pointer equality at runtime.
options.explanation: Swift continues using the custom == and hash(into:) implementations.

options.text: Two instances equal with == may produce different hashes, breaking lookups.
options.explanation: Right. Unequal hashes for equal objects violate the Hashable contract.

options.text: The dictionary ignores the extra property and hashes only the identifier.
options.explanation: Swift runs your custom hash(into:) code exactly as you wrote it.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
var fruits: [String: Int] = ["apple": 3, "banana": 5]
let result = fruits["orange", default: 0]
print(result)

options.text: 0, because the key does not exist and returns the default value.
options.explanation: Right. The default subscript returns 0 when the key is missing.

options.text: nil, because missing dictionary keys always produce nil values.
options.explanation: Using default: 0 returns an Int value of 0, not an optional.

options.text: 3, because orange adopts the count of the first key in the table.
options.explanation: Dictionary does not inherit values from existing keys.

options.text: It crashes at runtime due to an unrecognized dictionary key access.
options.explanation: Subscripting a dictionary never crashes on missing keys.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
var numbers: Set<Int> = [1, 2, 3]
let insertedFirst = numbers.insert(2).inserted
let insertedSecond = numbers.insert(4).inserted
print("\(insertedFirst) \(insertedSecond)")

options.text: true true, because both insert calls succeeded without compiler errors.
options.explanation: Inserting an existing element returns inserted: false.

options.text: false true, because 2 was already in the set and 4 was newly added.
options.explanation: Right. 2 was already present (false), while 4 was new (true).

options.text: false false, because Sets cannot be mutated once initialized.
options.explanation: The set is declared with var and mutates freely.

options.text: true false, because 2 was updated and 4 exceeded set capacity.
options.explanation: Set has dynamic capacity and 2 was not newly inserted.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

options.text: 2, because two separate struct instances were created and inserted.
options.explanation: Set enforces unique values. Equal items are not added twice.

options.text: 0, because inserting duplicate items resets the entire set storage.
options.explanation: Inserting duplicate items does not clear existing set items.

options.text: 1, because synthesized Hashable treats both instances as equal.
options.explanation: Right. Both structs have id: 10 and equal hashes, so count is 1.

options.text: It fails to compile because Item must define custom hash logic.
options.explanation: Swift synthesizes Hashable automatically when all properties conform.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
var counts: [String: Int] = ["swift": 1]
counts["swift"]? += 1
counts["objc"]? += 1
print("\(counts["swift"] ?? 0) \(counts["objc"] ?? 0)")

options.text: 2 1, because optional chaining inserts missing keys with value 1.
options.explanation: Optional chaining on nil fails quietly without inserting a key.

options.text: 1 0, because optional chaining cannot mutate dictionary values.
options.explanation: Optional chaining can mutate values when the key already exists.

options.text: 2 2, because missing keys are assigned the updated increment value.
options.explanation: counts['objc'] is nil, so counts['objc']? += 1 evaluates to nil.

options.text: 2 0, because optional chaining updates swift but ignores missing objc.
options.explanation: Right. 'swift' exists and becomes 2; 'objc' is nil and remains untouched.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

options.text: 3, because the closure resolves duplicate keys by keeping the second.
options.explanation: Right. The closure receives values 1 and 3, and selects 3.

options.text: 1, because the closure receives the first occurrence and keeps it.
options.explanation: The closure returns second, which evaluates to the newer value 3.

options.text: 4, because the closure adds the two duplicate numbers together.
options.explanation: The closure does not sum them; it returns second directly.

options.text: 0, because duplicate keys cause the dictionary initializer to drop key a.
options.explanation: The uniquingKeysWith closure resolves duplicates rather than dropping keys.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

options.text: Two Two, because missing keys return the most recently removed value.
options.explanation: Missing keys return nil, not the previous value.

options.text: Two nil, because key 2 was removed and key 3 was not present.
options.explanation: Right. removeValue returns the value if present, or nil if missing.

options.text: nil nil, because removeValue returns a boolean success indicator.
options.explanation: removeValue returns Value?, not a Bool.

options.text: It crashes at runtime when trying to remove key 3 from the dictionary.
options.explanation: removeValue safely returns nil when the key does not exist.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
let setA: Set<Int> = [1, 2, 3]
let setB: Set<Int> = [3, 4, 5]
let intersection = setA.intersection(setB)
print(intersection == [3])

options.text: false, because Set equality requires identical memory pointers.
options.explanation: Set equality checks member elements, not memory pointers.

options.text: false, because intersection returns elements unique to setA only.
options.explanation: subtracting returns unique elements; intersection returns shared elements.

options.text: true, because intersection keeps only elements present in both sets.
options.explanation: Right. The only value shared between setA and setB is 3.

options.text: It fails to compile because Set does not support array literal comparison.
options.explanation: Set conforms to ExpressibleByArrayLiteral and Equatable.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

options.text: 100, because reserveCapacity pads empty dictionary slots with nil.
options.explanation: reserveCapacity prepares bucket memory without adding elements.

options.text: 102, because the reservation adds 100 empty slots to the 2 existing ones.
options.explanation: Capacity reservation does not modify the count of elements.

options.text: 0, because reserving capacity resets and reinitializes the dictionary.
options.explanation: reserveCapacity preserves existing dictionary elements.

options.text: 2, because reserveCapacity allocates storage without adding elements.
options.explanation: Right. count reflects stored key-value pairs, which remains 2.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

questions.prompt: Explain how a hash table stores and retrieves values in O(1) average time. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a hash function converts keys into bucket indices in O(1) time.
Mentions that collisions occur when multiple keys map to the same bucket index.
States that Equatable comparison verifies the exact key during retrieval.

questions.modelAnswer: A hash table uses a hash function to turn each key into an integer hash value. It converts this hash value into a bucket index, allowing direct O(1) average access. When multiple keys produce the same bucket index, a collision happens. The hash table resolves collisions using open addressing or chaining, and uses Equatable checks to confirm the exact matching key.

questions.prompt: Explain the contract between Equatable and Hashable in Swift, and describe what happens if this contract is broken. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that equal instances (a == b) must produce identical hash values.
States that custom hash(into:) must hash the exact same properties checked in ==.
Explains that breaking the contract causes lost elements or failed lookups in sets and dictionaries.

questions.modelAnswer: The contract requires that if two instances are equal according to ==, they must produce the exact same hash value. When writing custom conformance, you must feed the same properties into hasher.combine that you inspect in ==. If this contract is broken, equal objects can hash into different buckets. This causes dictionaries and sets to lose elements or fail to find existing keys.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift randomize hash seeds on every app launch, and why must hashValue never be saved to disk? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift uses randomized seeds (SipHash) to prevent collision denial-of-service attacks.
States that hash values change each time the application launches.
Explains that persisting hashValue to disk or a database causes corrupt lookups on subsequent runs.

questions.modelAnswer: Swift uses SipHash with a per-process random seed to protect against collision denial-of-service attacks. Because the seed changes on every application launch, the hash value of any object is non-deterministic across runs. Persisting hashValue to disk or a network database will break after an app restart. Saved hash values will point to wrong buckets or fail to match in future sessions.

questions.prompt: Explain how a hash table optimizes the Two Sum problem from O(n^2) to O(n) time. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a dictionary stores numbers or indices as the array is traversed.
States that checking for target - current takes O(1) average lookup time.
Explains the trade-off: O(n) linear time achieved at the cost of O(n) auxiliary space.

questions.modelAnswer: A brute-force Two Sum solution tests every pair using nested loops, taking O(n^2) time. By using a hash table, we store visited numbers and their indices in a single pass. For each number, we check if the complement (target minus number) exists in the table in O(1) average time. This trades O(n) auxiliary space to achieve an optimal O(n) linear running time.

questions.prompt: What are the risks of mutating an object after adding it to a Set, and how do you prevent this issue? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that mutating properties alters the object's hash value or equality.
States that the mutated object remains in its original bucket, making it unfindable.
Recommends using immutable value types (structs with let properties) for set elements.

questions.modelAnswer: If an object is mutated after insertion into a Set, its hash value or equality check can change. The set does not move the object, leaving it trapped in its original bucket. Future contains and remove lookups will inspect the new bucket and fail to find the object. To prevent this issue, use immutable value types like structs with let properties for set members.

rubric.criterion: Declares the function with correct parameter type and return type.
Iterates through the characters of the string and counts frequencies using a dictionary.
Uses default dictionary subscripting or nil coalescing to handle missing keys cleanly.

questions.prompt: Write a function findTwoSum(_ numbers: [Int], target: Int) -> (Int, Int)? that returns the two numbers from the array that sum up to target, or nil if no pair exists. Use a Set to solve this in O(n) time.

rubric.criterion: Declares the function findTwoSum returning an optional tuple (Int, Int)?.
Uses a Set to track visited numbers and checks complement (target - number) in O(1) time.
Returns the matching pair when found, or returns nil if no pair satisfies the target.
